lines: Thunder shook the lectern so hard the shelves shivered in their corners, but everyone near me is still standing.
I checked books, shelves, and written names after the lightning, then counted heads. No one should be alone after a sky like that.
Near the lectern, the bell sounded small under that thunder. We stayed inside and kept the doors watched.
That thunder made everyone quiet. I checked the shelves twice.
The sky can keep its lightning. I have shelves to set right.
I checked paper, shelves, and lamp oil for sparks first, then checked faces for smoke and fear.
We passed water hand to hand and kept people away from the smoke. I checked the lectern after.
The books can wait. People come first.
We saved what we could reach around the lectern, then stopped pretending things matter more than neighbors.
The smoke is thinning near the lectern, but everyone is still sniffing the air like it might lie.
During a raid, the books can stay shelved; who makes it behind a door matters more.
The horns stopped, but my hands near the lectern still expect another wave from the road.
We counted living neighbors before books, shelves, and written names. That is the only count worth starting with.
Raiders came looking for easy emeralds. They found barred doors near the lectern and a bell that would not stop ringing.
From the lectern, I saw fear cross the square; then I saw courage get there first.
Night trouble tests the loose latch by the lectern first. We are fixing those before sunset.
I stayed near the quiet aisle by the lectern and listened for anyone calling from the dark.
Dawn gave the lectern enough light to count wounds, missing blocks, and who made it home.
The dark tested everyone. Most of us passed by keeping a note in the margin between us and teeth.
We are safe enough near the lectern, though every shadow is being inspected twice.
The wind threw sand through every crack. I am still cleaning dust out of the pages.
I checked books, shelves, and written names, then checked who was coughing too hard to answer.
Sand reached the lectern, the hinges, and half our eyes, but no one has been reported missing.
A hard wind teaches a librarian which doors actually close and which ones only pretend.
We are safe enough near the lectern, though the whole village sounds like it is chewing gravel.
The books can stay shelved. Warm hands, clear paths, and full hearths come first.
Snow piled against the doors, but everyone near the lectern found shelter.
Cold works quietly around the lectern. We are checking on anyone who stayed quiet too long.
I am clearing cold off the library floor and watching for footprints that stop too soon.
We are alright for now near the lectern. Keep the fires fed and the paths open.
